input: "The gallery, for a few minutes. I'd like to warm up before I have to defend my ears." I follow her down, keeping clear of the railing. "What's a good description of flight, then? What did your tutors leave out?" I ask it as an ordinary question, without asking her to demonstrate.
output:
The covered gallery lies one level below the terrace, sheltered by a roof of dark slate and stormward panes of thick, wavering glass. Lightning moves through them in silent white branches. Two bronze braziers breathe coal heat into the cold, enough that your hands begin to remember themselves.

Ysolde stops beside the central window. For a while she watches the storm without opening her notebook.

“They left out the labor,” she says at last. “A wing is not an idea. It aches. Bad air travels through every bone, and one can be very large and still make an undignified landing.”

There is the faintest change at the corner of her mouth.

“My tutors described lift, altitude, the risks of icing at height. All useful. None of them wrote about sunlight on another dragon’s scales, or the way a valley looks when it stops being a place and becomes a line beneath you.”

Lightning flares blue across her pale face. She folds her arms within her cloak.

“I used to think flight was freedom. It is not exactly that.” She considers the glass, the storm, perhaps the word itself. “It is complete occupation. There is no room to be an heir properly, or improperly. There is only weather, distance, and not striking a mountain.”

A softer gust rattles the panes.

“People often ask whether I will show them,” she adds. “They usually mean well. It becomes an invitation with several witnesses and an interpretation prepared in advance.” Her grey eyes turn to you. “Thank you for asking what it is instead.”

Below, a vein of lightning opens through the clouds and fades.

“Your imaginary people,” Ysolde says. “When they fly, do they do it to escape what troubles them, or to see its shape from above?”
